archetype.name: Point Guard (checkdown-heavy)
archetype.definition: A year-two distributor who works the short and intermediate field, spreads the ball across four or five targets, protects himself from sacks and uses his legs on broken plays, but has not yet made the deep ball part of his game.

report.headline: Cleaner and safer in year two, but still living below the sticks
report.take:
Cam Ward's second season is a story of a quarterback who fixed the obvious rookie problems and has not yet found the next gear. The 2025 film showed a holder: 3.0 seconds to throw, a 32.2% pressure-to-sack rate and bad throws on 17.6% of attempts. This year the clock is down to 2.8, pressure turns into a sack only 18.6% of the time (7th of 42), his 4.7% sack rate ranks 9th, and the bad-throw rate is down 4.4 points. Completion percentage is up 4 points and CPOE up 2.5. That is real development in processing and ball placement, not noise, because it shows up across several independent measures at once.

The cost is that he's gotten safer by getting shorter. Intended air yards sit at 6.71, he throws 2.5 yards short of the sticks on average, and his aggressiveness fell from 12.6% to 10.1%. The result is a 5.97 yards-per-attempt mark that ranks 42nd of 54, barely better than last year's 5.87. The damage is concentrated in two places: throws behind the line of scrimmage have cost 14.7 EPA in total, much of it on Tony Pollard targets (-10.7 EPA on 30 targets), and the deep ball has been a dead zone, 5 completions-level territory at 19.2% with a -19.5 CPOE on 26 attempts. Meanwhile the 10-19 yard window is his best area by far at +0.285 EPA per attempt. The quarterback the numbers describe is good at the middle of the field and is choosing it too rarely.

Third down is where all of this comes due. He faces an average of 8.2 yards to go, throws short of the marker by habit, and converts just 28%, with third-down plays alone costing 20 EPA, roughly his entire season deficit. Some of that is the offense around him (26th in EPA) and a defense that ranks 29th, which keeps him chasing. But the clutch split argues the talent is there: in close fourth quarters he's at +0.273 EPA per play with a +5.2 CPOE, while one-score situations overall drain -26.6 EPA. When the game forces him to push the ball, he does it well.

The last three games are the most encouraging stretch of his career: +0.057 EPA per dropback, a 1.8 CPOE and 238.7 passing yards a game, with aggressiveness spiking to 16-17% against Cleveland and Cincinnati. The Jacksonville game pulled back to checkdowns (5.1% aggressive, 5.6 intended air yards) and a negative EPA despite clean volume, which shows the default is still conservative. The direction is right; the question is whether the coaching staff and his supporting cast let him keep throwing into that intermediate window.

strengths.title: Intermediate window is his best area
strengths.body: Throws of 10-19 air yards are producing +0.285 EPA per attempt and 17.7 EPA in total, the only depth bucket carrying his passing game. That comes from improved timing and placement on in-breakers and outs rather than raw arm talent. It's a repeatable skill, and it's the area the offense should be leaning on more.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance transformed from rookie year
strengths.body: Pressure becomes a sack 18.6% of the time, down from 32.2% as a rookie, and his 4.7% sack rate is well under the 7.9% league average. A quicker clock and fewer bad throws show he's processing faster rather than just dumping the ball blindly. Gains like this tend to stick because they're habits, not luck.

strengths.title: Legs add real value
strengths.body: His 20 scrambles average +0.437 EPA with 7 first downs, and the handful of designed runs have been efficient too. Rushing output is up 7.4 yards a game over last year, and it's a floor-raiser in weeks the passing game stalls. Expect it to hold as long as he's healthy.

concerns.title: Third downs are sinking drives
concerns.body: A 28% conversion rate and -20 EPA in total on third down account for most of his season deficit. Long distances (8.2 yards to go on average) set it up, but throwing 2.5 yards short of the sticks finishes it. This is a real flaw in approach more than ability, and the strong close-game fourth-quarter numbers suggest it's fixable if he's asked to attack.

concerns.title: Screens and backfield dumps bleed value
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have cost 14.7 EPA with a 23.1% success rate, and Pollard's targets alone are -10.7 EPA. Part of that is scheme and the back's usage, not Ward's decisions, but he's also leaning on them as a release valve. It will persist while the offense calls it this much.

concerns.title: No deep ball yet
concerns.body: On 26 deep attempts he's at 19.2% completions, a -19.5 CPOE and two interceptions, without a touchdown. The sample is small, but the shrinking aggressiveness and a rookie season with similar yards per attempt say this isn't just bad luck. Until it changes, defenses can squeeze everything short.

trend.note: After a Week 5-6 trough (-14.2 EPA against Houston, a -20.1 CPOE at Indianapolis), the last three games run +0.123 EPA per dropback above his season with far more volume. Jacksonville's checkdown-heavy, negative-EPA outing is a reminder the climb is uneven.

nextGame.headline: Worst defense in the league, and a likely shootout
nextGame.body:
Dallas ranks 32nd in defensive EPA and 31st against the pass, allows 20.3 PPR points a game to quarterbacks (30th) and is 29th on short throws, exactly where Ward lives. The one area it holds up is deep (10th), which barely touches a quarterback who rarely completes those throws anyway. With Dallas's offense 5th in EPA, a 54.5 total and Tennessee an 8.5-point underdog, the script should push him into the trailing, high-volume mode where his recent production has come. One caution: offenses run more than usual against Dallas, and Tennessee already leans run, so early downs may go to the backfield.

Availability tilts both ways. Dallas is without CB DaRon Bland (89% of snaps) and safety P.J. Locke, thinning a secondary that already gives WR1s 6.8 PPR points over their averages, the worst mark in the league. On his side, Carnell Tate, his most efficient target at +0.172 EPA per target, is listed out with a shoulder injury but the coach is hopeful he returns; Wan'Dale Robinson's ankle leaves the slot uncertain; and left guard Peter Skoronski (97% of snaps) is on IR, which weakens the interior against a pass rush that is only middling.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs a leaky underneath defense
keyMatchups.body: Dallas allows +0.186 EPA on short passes, 29th in the league, and Ward's 0-9 yard throws are completing 72.1% with a positive CPOE. This is the rare week where his conservative tendencies should still produce efficient drives. It also makes the screen game less costly than usual.

keyMatchups.title: Tate's return vs a thin secondary
keyMatchups.body: If Tate plays, he becomes the WR1 against a defense that lets that role exceed its averages by more than any other team, now without Bland. If he sits, the targets go to Robinson and Ayomanor, a less efficient mix, and the ceiling drops.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script
keyMatchups.body: Dallas's offense ranks 5th in EPA and the 54.5 total is far above anything Ward has played in this year. Trailing scripts have pushed him to his best volume weeks, like the 304-yard game at Cincinnati with a 45.5 total.

nextGame.watch: Whether he attacks the 10-19 yard window on early downs or retreats to checkdowns like he did against Jacksonville.

restOfSeason.body:
The year-two gains in sack avoidance, accuracy and bad-throw rate look durable, and his rushing adds a steady floor. With a bottom-four defense behind him, he'll keep seeing pass-heavy trailing scripts, which should keep volume near his recent level. The efficiency ceiling is set by depth: until he hits more intermediate and deep throws, yards per attempt will stay below league average and third downs will keep killing drives. Expect roughly 205-250 passing yards a game, about one to one-and-a-half touchdowns, and 15-28 rushing yards.

What likely regresses: the close-fourth-quarter magic (+0.273 EPA) on 46 plays will cool, while the deep-ball futility on 26 attempts should improve somewhat just on volume. Receiver health matters more than anything, since Tate is the one target turning his throws into positive value, and Skoronski's absence until December takes away a reliable interior blocker.
swingFactors: Carnell Tate's shoulder and Robinson's ankle
Willingness to throw past the sticks on third down

confidence.note: Nine starts that match his rookie profile; receiver health and a three-game uptick add uncertainty.
